reminder: A best approximation of a point from a set is an element of the set that is nearest to the point.
definition: Let $X$ be a [normed space](c:normed-space), let $M$ be a [subset](c:subset) of $X$ and let $x\in X$. An element $m_0\in M$ is a best approximation of $x$ in $M$ when $\|x-m_0\|=\inf_{m\in M}\|x-m\|$, so $m_0$ attains the [distance](c:distance) from $x$ to $M$.
examples: In $\mathbb R^2$ with the Euclidean norm, the point $(3,0)$ is the best approximation of $(3,4)$ in the $x$-axis.
For a closed subspace $M$ of a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space), the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $M$ is the unique best approximation of $x$ in $M$.
In $C[0,1]$ with the supremum norm, every function has a best approximation among the polynomials of degree at most $n$.
Non-example: The number $0$ has no best approximation in the open interval $(1,2)$ of $\mathbb R$, because no point of $(1,2)$ reaches the distance $1$.

reminder: The $n$-th Betti number of a chain complex is the rank of its $n$-th homology.
definition: Let $V$ be a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) of [modules](c:module) over a [ring](c:ring) $R$. Its $n$-th Betti number is the [rank](c:rank) of the $n$-th [homology](c:homology) module $H_n(V)$. For a space $X$, the number $b_n(X)$ is the rank of the singular homology group $H_n(X;\mathbb Z)$.
examples: The circle $S^1$ has $b_0=1$, $b_1=1$ and $b_n=0$ for $n\ge2$.
The torus has the Betti numbers $1,2,1$ in degrees $0,1,2$.
The sphere $S^2$ has $b_0=1$, $b_1=0$ and $b_2=1$.
Non-example: The group $H_1(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/2$ gives no Betti number, because torsion has rank $0$, so $b_1(\mathbb{RP}^2)=0$.

reminder: A bicategory is a category with 2-morphisms in which composition is associative and unital only up to coherent isomorphism.
definition: A bicategory has objects, 1-morphisms between objects and [2-morphisms](c:2-morphism) between 1-morphisms. For any two objects, the 1-morphisms and 2-morphisms form a [category](c:category), and composition of 1-morphisms is a [functor](c:functor) between these hom-categories. Composition is associative and unital only up to specified invertible 2-morphisms, the associators and unitors, and these satisfy the pentagon and triangle identities.
examples: Rings, bimodules and bimodule homomorphisms form a bicategory, because the tensor product of bimodules is associative only up to natural isomorphism.
Sets, spans of sets and maps of spans form a bicategory, because composition of spans uses pullbacks that are unique only up to isomorphism.
A [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) is a bicategory with exactly one object.
Non-example: Data with invertible associators that do not satisfy the pentagon identity is not a bicategory.

steps: Take a [2-category](c:2-category), where composition of 1-morphisms is strictly associative and unital.
Choose identity 2-morphisms as the associators and unitors.
The pentagon and triangle identities then hold, because every side of each diagram is an identity.
So the 2-category is a bicategory whose coherence isomorphisms are identities.
links.why: Every result about bicategories applies to strict 2-categories such as the 2-category of categories.

steps: Take a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) $(M,\otimes,I)$ and a single object $*$.
Let the hom-category from $*$ to $*$ be $M$, with composition given by $\otimes$ and the identity 1-morphism given by $I$.
The associator and unitors of $M$ serve as the associator and unitors of the bicategory.
The pentagon and triangle identities of $M$ are exactly those of the bicategory.
links.why: A monoidal category is a one-object bicategory, so theorems about bicategories apply to it.

reminder: A bicharacteristic of a symbol is an integral curve of its Hamiltonian vector field that lies in its zero set.
definition: Let $p$ be the real [principal symbol](c:principal-symbol) of a differential operator on a manifold $X$, so $p$ is a smooth function on the [cotangent bundle](c:cotangent-bundle) $T^*X$ without its zero section. A bicharacteristic of $p$ is an integral curve of the [Hamiltonian vector field](c:hamiltonian-vector-field) $H_p$ that lies in the characteristic set $\{p=0\}$, taken up to reparametrization. Because $H_pp=0$, an integral curve that meets $\{p=0\}$ stays in it.
examples: For the transport operator $\partial_t+v\cdot\nabla_x$ with symbol $\tau+v\cdot\xi$, the bicharacteristics are the lines $x=x_0+vt$ with constant covector $(\tau,\xi)$ that satisfies $\tau+v\cdot\xi=0$.
For the wave operator $\partial_t^2-\Delta$ with symbol $|\xi|^2-\tau^2$, each bicharacteristic projects to a light ray, a straight line of speed $1$ in spacetime.
Non-example: For the wave symbol, an integral curve of $H_p$ on which $p=1$ is not a bicharacteristic, because it does not lie in the characteristic set $\{p=0\}$.

reminder: A bifibration is a functor that is both a Grothendieck fibration and a Grothendieck opfibration.
definition: A [functor](c:functor) $p:E\to B$ is a bifibration when it is a [Grothendieck fibration](c:grothendieck-fibration) and also a Grothendieck opfibration. That is, every morphism $f:b\to b'$ of $B$ has a [Cartesian lift](c:cartesian-morphism) at every object over $b'$, and a cocartesian lift at every object over $b$.
examples: For a category $C$ with pullbacks, the codomain functor $\mathrm{cod}:C^{\to}\to C$ is a bifibration: pullback gives the Cartesian lifts and composition gives the cocartesian lifts.
The functor from pairs $(R,M)$ of a ring and an $R$-module to rings is a bifibration: restriction of scalars gives Cartesian lifts and extension of scalars gives cocartesian lifts.
The functor from pairs $(X,A)$ of a set and a subset to sets is a bifibration: preimage gives Cartesian lifts and image gives cocartesian lifts.
Non-example: Let $C$ be the poset $x\to z\leftarrow y$. Then $\mathrm{cod}:C^{\to}\to C$ is not a fibration, because $y\to z$ has no pullback along $x\to z$.

steps: Take a bifibration $p:E\to B$.
By definition, $p$ is a [Grothendieck fibration](c:grothendieck-fibration), so every morphism of $B$ has Cartesian lifts.
Forget the cocartesian lifts that $p$ also has.
The bifibration adds the condition that every morphism of $B$ also has cocartesian lifts.
links.why: Every fact about Grothendieck fibrations, such as the pullback functors between fibers, holds for a bifibration, which also has pushforward functors.

reminder: A big and nef divisor has nonnegative degree on every curve and a positive top self-intersection number.
definition: Let $D$ be a Cartier [divisor](c:divisor), with rational or real coefficients allowed, on a projective [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) $X$ of dimension $n$. It is nef if the [intersection number](c:intersection-number) $D\cdot C$ is at least $0$ for every curve $C$ in $X$. A nef divisor is also big exactly when $D^n>0$, which means that $h^0(X,mD)$ grows like $m^n$.
examples: Every [ample divisor](c:ample-divisor) is nef and big, for example a hyperplane class on $\mathbb P^n$.

Let $\pi:\mathrm{Bl}_p\mathbb P^2\to\mathbb P^2$ be the blow-up at a point and let $H$ be a line class. Then $\pi^*H$ is nef and big, but it is not ample, because it has degree $0$ on the exceptional curve.
Non-example: On $\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1$, the fiber class $F$ of a projection is nef, but $F^2=0$, so it is not big.

steps: Take an [ample divisor](c:ample-divisor) $D$ on a projective variety $X$ of dimension $n$.
By the Nakai-Moishezon criterion, $D^{\dim V}\cdot V>0$ for every subvariety $V$ of positive dimension.
For a curve $V=C$ this gives $D\cdot C>0$, so $D$ is nef.
For $V=X$ it gives $D^n>0$, so $D$ is big.
links.why: Results about nef and big divisors, such as vanishing theorems, apply to every ample divisor.

steps: Take a nef and big divisor $D$ and its line bundle $\mathcal O_X(D)$.
The degree of $\mathcal O_X(D)$ on a curve $C$ is $D\cdot C$, and this is at least $0$.
So $\mathcal O_X(D)$ is a [nef line bundle](c:nef-line-bundle).
Bigness adds the condition $D^n>0$.
links.why: Facts about nef line bundles apply to the divisor, and bigness adds a positive volume.

reminder: The Boltzmann equation gives how the density of a dilute gas changes through free flight and binary collisions.
definition: The Boltzmann equation is the [partial differential equation](c:partial-differential-equation) $\partial_tf+v\cdot\nabla_xf=Q(f,f)$ for the density $f(t,x,v)\ge0$ of a dilute gas at time $t$, position $x$ and velocity $v$. The collision operator is $Q(f,f)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{S^2}B\,(f'f'_*-ff_*)\,d\omega\,dv_*$, an [integral](c:integral) that counts the gain and the loss of particles of velocity $v$ through binary collisions. Here $B\ge0$ is the collision kernel, and $f'$ and $f'_*$ are evaluated at the velocities after the collision.
examples: A Maxwellian $f=\rho(2\pi T)^{-3/2}e^{-|v-u|^2/(2T)}$ with constant $\rho$, $T$ and $u$ solves the equation, because $\partial_tf=0$, $\nabla_xf=0$ and $Q(f,f)=0$.
For a gas with the same density at every position, the equation reduces to the spatially homogeneous equation $\partial_tf=Q(f,f)$.
Non-example: The free transport equation $\partial_tf+v\cdot\nabla_xf=0$ has no collision term, so it is not the Boltzmann equation; it describes particles that never collide.

reminder: A Boolean circuit is an acyclic network of AND, OR and NOT gates that computes a Boolean function.
definition: A Boolean circuit with $n$ inputs is a finite directed acyclic graph. Its source nodes carry the input variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ or constants, every other node is a [logic gate](c:logic-gate) (AND, OR or NOT) that reads the nodes that point to it, and one node is the output. The circuit computes the [Boolean function](c:boolean-function) $\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ that gives the value of the output node.
examples: One AND gate with the inputs $x_1$ and $x_2$ is a circuit that computes $x_1\wedge x_2$.
The circuit $(x_1\vee x_2)\wedge\neg(x_1\wedge x_2)$ uses four gates and computes the parity of two bits.
Every Boolean function of $n$ bits has a circuit, for example one built from its disjunctive normal form.
Non-example: A network in which the output of an AND gate feeds back into its own input has a cycle, so it is not a Boolean circuit.

reminder: A Boolean function of $n$ variables is a function from $n$-tuples of bits to one bit.
definition: A Boolean function of $n$ variables is a [function](c:function) $f:\mathbb B^n\to\mathbb B$, where $\mathbb B=\{0,1\}$ is the Boolean domain and $\mathbb B^n$ is the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) of $n$ copies of $\mathbb B$. There are $2^{2^n}$ such functions, one for each truth table.
examples: The function $\mathrm{AND}(x,y)=xy$ on $\mathbb B^2$.
The parity function $x_1\oplus\cdots\oplus x_n$ on $\mathbb B^n$.
The majority function on three bits, which has the value $1$ when at least two inputs are $1$.
Non-example: The map $\mathbb B^2\to\mathbb N$, $(x,y)\mapsto x+y$, takes the value $2$, so it is not a Boolean function.

steps: Take a [Boolean-valued function](c:boolean-valued-function) $g:X\to\mathbb B$ on any set $X$.
Choose the domain $X=\mathbb B^n$ for some $n$.
Then $g$ is a Boolean function of $n$ variables.
So a Boolean function is the case where the domain is a power of $\mathbb B$.
links.why: Facts about Boolean-valued functions, such as indicator functions of subsets, apply to Boolean functions.

reminder: A Borel measure is a measure that is defined on all Borel sets of a topological space.
definition: Let $X$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space) and let $\mathcal B(X)$ be the family of [Borel sets](c:borel-set) of $X$, the smallest [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) that contains every [open set](c:open-set). A Borel measure on $X$ is a [measure](c:measure) $\mu:\mathcal B(X)\to[0,\infty]$, so $\mu(\emptyset)=0$ and $\mu$ is countably additive.
examples: Lebesgue measure, restricted to the Borel sets of $\mathbb R^n$.
The Dirac measure $\delta_x$ at a point $x$ of any topological space.
The counting measure on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R$.
Non-example: The signed measure $\delta_0-\delta_1$ on $\mathbb R$ has the value $-1$ on $\{1\}$, so it is not a Borel measure.

steps: Take a Borel measure $\mu$ on a topological space $X$.
By definition, $\mu$ is a countably additive function on $\mathcal B(X)$ with $\mu(\emptyset)=0$.
So $(X,\mathcal B(X),\mu)$ is a measure space, and $\mu$ is a [measure](c:measure).
The Borel case adds that the sigma-algebra is the one generated by the open sets.
links.why: Every fact about measures, such as monotone convergence, holds for Borel measures.

steps: Take a [Radon measure](c:radon-measure) $\mu$ on a topological space $X$.
In the usual definition, $\mu$ is a Borel measure that is also locally finite and regular.
Forget the local finiteness and the regularity.
What remains is a Borel measure, and the counting measure on $\mathbb R$ shows that it need not be locally finite.
links.why: Results for Borel measures apply to Radon measures, and Radon measures add the regularity that makes them useful on nice spaces.

reminder: A Bott element is a unit of nonzero degree in the coefficient ring of a periodic cohomology theory.
definition: Let $E$ be a multiplicative [periodic cohomology theory](c:periodic-cohomology-theory) with coefficient ring $E^\bullet=E^\bullet(\mathrm{pt})$. A Bott element is an [invertible element](c:invertible) $\beta\in E^d$ of nonzero degree $d$, so multiplication by $\beta$ is an isomorphism $E^n(X)\to E^{n+d}(X)$ for every space $X$ and every $n$.
examples: In complex [topological K-theory](c:topological-k-theory), the class $\beta=[H]-1$ of the tautological line bundle $H$ over $S^2=\mathbb{CP}^1$, minus the trivial bundle, is a Bott element of degree $2$ or $-2$, depending on the sign convention.
The coefficient ring of complex K-theory is $\mathbb Z[\beta,\beta^{-1}]$.
Real K-theory has a Bott element in degree $8$.
Non-example: Ordinary cohomology with integer coefficients is not periodic; its coefficient ring $\mathbb Z$ lies in degree $0$, so it has no unit of nonzero degree.

reminder: A bounded holomorphic function is a holomorphic function whose absolute value stays below a fixed constant.
definition: Let $U$ be an open subset of $\mathbb C$, for example the [unit disc](c:unit-disc). A bounded holomorphic function on $U$ is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) $f:U\to\mathbb C$ that is also a [bounded function](c:bounded-function), that is $\sup_{z\in U}|f(z)|<\infty$. These functions form the Banach algebra $H^\infty(U)$ under the supremum norm.
examples: Every power $z^n$ is a bounded holomorphic function on the unit disc, because $|z^n|<1$ there.
The function $1/(2-z)$ is holomorphic on the unit disc, and $|1/(2-z)|\le1$ there.
The function $e^{iz}$ on the upper half-plane satisfies $|e^{iz}|=e^{-\operatorname{Im}z}\le1$.
Non-example: The function $1/(1-z)$ is holomorphic on the unit disc, but $1/(1-r)\to\infty$ as $r\to1^-$, so it is not bounded.

steps: Take a bounded holomorphic function $f$ on an open set $U$.
By definition, $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $U$.
So $f$ is a holomorphic function.
The bounded case adds the condition $\sup_U|f|<\infty$.
links.why: Every theorem about holomorphic functions, such as Cauchy's formula, applies to bounded holomorphic functions.

steps: Take a bounded holomorphic function $f:U\to\mathbb C$.
Its values satisfy $|f(z)|\le M$ for some constant $M$ and all $z\in U$.
So $f$ is a [bounded function](c:bounded-function) on $U$.
The holomorphic case adds that $f$ is complex differentiable at every point of $U$.
links.why: Holomorphy adds tools such as the maximum principle and the Cauchy estimates to the bound.

reminder: A series has bounded partial sums when its sequence of partial sums stays within a fixed bound.
definition: A [series](c:series) $\sum_{k\ge1}a_k$ has bounded partial sums when there is a constant $M$ with $\bigl|\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_k\bigr|\le M$ for every $n$, where each sum is a [partial sum](c:partial-sum) of the series. The series does not need to converge.
examples: The series $\sum(-1)^k$ has the partial sums $-1,0,-1,0,\dots$, which are bounded, although the series diverges.
Every convergent series has bounded partial sums, for example $\sum1/k^2$.
For $x\notin2\pi\mathbb Z$, the partial sums of $\sum\sin(kx)$ are bounded by $1/|\sin(x/2)|$.
Non-example: The harmonic series $\sum1/k$ has the partial sums $1+\tfrac12+\cdots+\tfrac1n$, which grow without bound.

reminder: BPP is the class of problems that a probabilistic polynomial-time machine solves with error at most one third.
definition: BPP is the [complexity class](c:complexity-class) of languages $L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*$ for which a randomized [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) $M$ exists that halts within polynomial [time](c:time-complexity) on every input. For every input $x$, it must give $\Pr[M(x)=1]\ge2/3$ if $x\in L$ and $\Pr[M(x)=1]\le1/3$ if $x\notin L$.
examples: Every language in P is in BPP, because a deterministic machine is a randomized machine with error $0$.
The set of prime numbers is in BPP, by the Miller-Rabin test repeated enough times.
Testing whether an arithmetic circuit computes the zero polynomial is in BPP, by evaluating the circuit at random points.
Non-example: The halting problem is not in BPP, because it is undecidable and a deterministic machine could simulate every coin flip of such a machine.

reminder: A braided monoidal category is a monoidal category with a natural isomorphism $X\otimes Y\cong Y\otimes X$ that satisfies the hexagon identities.
definition: A braided monoidal category is a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) $(C,\otimes,I)$ with a [braiding](c:braiding), a [natural isomorphism](c:natural-isomorphism) $\beta_{X,Y}:X\otimes Y\to Y\otimes X$. The braiding satisfies the two hexagon identities, which make it compatible with the associator: braiding $X$ past $Y\otimes Z$ equals braiding $X$ past $Y$ and then past $Z$, and likewise for braiding $X\otimes Y$ past $Z$.
examples: Every symmetric monoidal category is braided, for example vector spaces with the flip map $v\otimes w\mapsto w\otimes v$.
Representations of a quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ form a braided monoidal category, with the braiding given by the universal R-matrix; it is not symmetric in general.
The category of braids is braided, and its braiding is the crossing of two strands.

Non-example: For a nonabelian group $G$, the monoidal category of $G$-graded vector spaces has no braiding, because $\delta_g\otimes\delta_h=\delta_{gh}$ and $\delta_h\otimes\delta_g=\delta_{hg}$ differ when $gh\ne hg$.

steps: Take a braided monoidal category $(C,\otimes,I,\beta)$.
Forget the braiding $\beta$.
What remains is a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) $(C,\otimes,I)$.
The braided case adds a natural isomorphism $\beta$ that satisfies the hexagon identities.
links.why: Every fact about monoidal categories holds in a braided one, which also lets you swap tensor factors.

steps: Take a [symmetric monoidal category](c:symmetric-monoidal-category) with the symmetry $\sigma_{X,Y}:X\otimes Y\to Y\otimes X$.
The symmetry is a natural isomorphism that satisfies the hexagon identities.
So $\sigma$ is a braiding, and the category is braided.
The symmetric case adds the condition $\sigma_{Y,X}\circ\sigma_{X,Y}=\mathrm{id}$.
links.why: A theorem about braided monoidal categories applies to every symmetric monoidal category, such as vector spaces.

reminder: The Brauer group of a commutative ring is the group of Morita classes of Azumaya algebras under the tensor product.
definition: For a commutative [ring](c:ring) $R$, the Brauer group $\mathrm{Br}(R)$ is the set of [Morita equivalence](c:morita-equivalence) classes of [Azumaya algebras](c:azumaya-algebra) over $R$. It is an abelian [group](c:group) with the product $[A][B]=[A\otimes_RB]$, the identity $[R]$, and the inverse $[A]^{-1}=[A^{\mathrm{op}}]$.
examples: $\mathrm{Br}(\mathbb C)=0$, and $\mathrm{Br}(\mathbb F_q)=0$ for every finite field $\mathbb F_q$.
$\mathrm{Br}(\mathbb R)=\mathbb Z/2$, generated by the class of the quaternions $\mathbb H$.
$\mathrm{Br}(\mathbb Q_p)\cong\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ for every prime $p$.

Non-example: The field $\mathbb C$ is a division algebra over $\mathbb R$ but not an Azumaya algebra over $\mathbb R$, because its center is $\mathbb C$, so it gives no class in $\mathrm{Br}(\mathbb R)$.

reminder: For a prime $p$, the Brown-Peterson spectrum is the summand of $p$-local complex cobordism with homotopy ring $\mathbb Z_{(p)}[v_1,v_2,\dots]$.
definition: Fix a [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$. The [localization](c:bousfield-localization-of-spectra) $MU_{(p)}$ of [complex cobordism](c:complex-cobordism) at $p$ splits as a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) of suspensions of one spectrum, and this summand is the Brown-Peterson spectrum $BP$. It is a ring spectrum with $\pi_*BP\cong\mathbb Z_{(p)}[v_1,v_2,\dots]$, where $|v_n|=2(p^n-1)$.
examples: For $p=2$, the generators $v_1,v_2,v_3$ have the degrees $2,6,14$.
For $p=3$, the generator $v_1$ has degree $4$.
Non-example: The spectrum $MU_{(p)}$ is not $BP$, because $\pi_*MU_{(p)}$ has a polynomial generator in every positive even degree, not only in the degrees $2(p^n-1)$.

reminder: The Busemann function of a ray $\gamma$ is the limit of $t-d(x,\gamma(t))$ as $t$ goes to infinity.
definition: Let $M$ be a complete [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) with [distance](c:distance) $d$, and let $\gamma:[0,\infty)\to M$ be a ray, that is a [geodesic](c:geodesic) with $d(\gamma(s),\gamma(t))=|s-t|$ for all $s,t$. The Busemann function of $\gamma$ is $b_\gamma(x)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\bigl(t-d(x,\gamma(t))\bigr)$. The limit exists, because $t-d(x,\gamma(t))$ does not decrease in $t$ and is bounded above by $d(x,\gamma(0))$.
examples: In $\mathbb R^n$, the ray $\gamma(t)=tu$ with $|u|=1$ has the Busemann function $b_\gamma(x)=\langle x,u\rangle$.
In the hyperbolic upper half-plane, the ray $t\mapsto(0,e^t)$ has the Busemann function $b(x,y)=\ln y$, so its level sets are horocycles.
Non-example: On the round sphere $S^2$ there is no ray, because every geodesic stops minimizing after length $\pi$, so no Busemann function is defined.

reminder: A Hilbert C*-module is a complete right module over a C*-algebra with an algebra-valued inner product.
definition: Let $A$ be a [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra). A Hilbert $A$-module is a right $A$-[module](c:module) $E$ with an $A$-valued [inner product](c:inner-product-space) $\langle x,y\rangle_A$ that is linear in $y$ and satisfies $\langle x,ya\rangle_A=\langle x,y\rangle_Aa$ and $\langle x,y\rangle_A^*=\langle y,x\rangle_A$. Moreover, $\langle x,x\rangle_A\ge0$ with equality only for $x=0$, and $E$ is complete in the norm $\|x\|=\|\langle x,x\rangle_A\|^{1/2}$.
examples: The algebra $A$ itself, with $\langle x,y\rangle_A=x^*y$.
The space $\ell^2(A)$ of sequences $(a_n)$ for which $\sum a_n^*a_n$ converges in norm, with $\langle x,y\rangle_A=\sum x_n^*y_n$.
A complex Hilbert space is a Hilbert $\mathbb C$-module.
Non-example: The space of finitely supported sequences in $A\ne0$, with the same inner product, satisfies the other axioms but is not complete, so it is not a Hilbert module.

steps: Take a complex [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ and the C*-algebra $A=\mathbb C$.
A right $\mathbb C$-module is a complex vector space, and the inner product of $H$ is a $\mathbb C$-valued inner product with the required properties.
Here $\|\langle x,x\rangle\|^{1/2}$ equals the norm of $H$, so completeness of the module is completeness of $H$.
So $H$ is a Hilbert $\mathbb C$-module, and a general $C^*$-algebra $A$ replaces the scalars $\mathbb C$.
links.why: Hilbert modules extend the language of Hilbert spaces to modules over C*-algebras, although some facts, such as orthogonal complements, can fail.

reminder: The Calkin algebra is the quotient of the bounded operators on a Hilbert space by the compact operators.
definition: Let $H$ be an infinite-dimensional separable complex [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space). The Calkin algebra is the quotient $B(H)/K(H)$ of the [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) $B(H)$ of [bounded operators](c:bounded-operator) by the closed [ideal](c:ideal) $K(H)$ of [compact operators](c:compact-operator). It is again a C*-algebra, with the quotient norm.
examples: An operator $T$ is Fredholm exactly when its image in the Calkin algebra is invertible, which is Atkinson's theorem.
The essential spectrum of $T$ is the spectrum of its image in the Calkin algebra.
The Calkin algebra is simple, because $K(H)$ is the only nonzero proper closed ideal of $B(H)$ for separable $H$.
Non-example: For finite-dimensional $H$, every operator is compact, so $B(H)/K(H)=0$; this is not the Calkin algebra, which needs $H$ to be infinite-dimensional.

steps: Take the C*-algebra $B(H)$ and its closed two-sided ideal $K(H)$ of compact operators.
The quotient of a [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) by a closed two-sided ideal is again a C*-algebra, with the quotient norm.
So $B(H)/K(H)$ is a C*-algebra.
The Calkin algebra is the case of the algebra $B(H)$ and the ideal $K(H)$.
links.why: Results about C*-algebras, such as the Gelfand-Naimark representation theorem, apply to the Calkin algebra.

reminder: On a smooth variety of dimension $n$, the canonical sheaf is the sheaf of $n$-forms.
definition: For a smooth [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) $X$ of dimension $n$, the canonical sheaf is the [sheaf](c:sheaf) $\omega_X=\Omega^n_X=\bigwedge^n\Omega_X$ of $n$-forms, the top exterior power of the sheaf of [Kähler differentials](c:kahler-differential). For a normal variety $X$, it is $j_*\omega_U$, where $j:U\to X$ is the inclusion of the smooth locus.
examples: On projective space, $\omega_{\mathbb P^n}\cong\mathcal O(-n-1)$.
On an elliptic curve $E$, $\omega_E\cong\mathcal O_E$.
On a smooth hypersurface of degree $d$ in $\mathbb P^n$, $\omega\cong\mathcal O(d-n-1)$, by the adjunction formula.
Non-example: The sheaf of $1$-forms $\Omega_X$ on a smooth surface $X$ has rank $2$, so it is not the canonical sheaf, which is the line bundle $\bigwedge^2\Omega_X$.

steps: Take a smooth variety $X$ of dimension $n$ and its [canonical bundle](c:canonical-bundle), the line bundle $\bigwedge^nT^*X$.
The sheaf of sections of this line bundle is $\Omega^n_X$, which is the canonical sheaf.
So the canonical bundle of a smooth variety determines the canonical sheaf.
The sheaf $j_*\omega_U$ is also defined on a normal variety, where it need not come from a line bundle.
links.why: Statements about the canonical sheaf cover the canonical bundle and extend to singular varieties.

reminder: Cantor space is the space of infinite binary sequences with the product topology, and it is homeomorphic to the middle-thirds Cantor set.
definition: Cantor space is the [topological space](c:topological-space) $2^{\mathbb N}=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ of infinite binary sequences with the [product topology](c:product-topology), where each factor $\{0,1\}$ is discrete. Up to [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism), it is the Cantor set obtained from $[0,1]$ by removing open middle thirds again and again. A nonempty compact metrizable space is homeomorphic to it exactly when the space is perfect and totally disconnected.
examples: The middle-thirds Cantor set: the numbers in $[0,1]$ that have a ternary expansion with only the digits $0$ and $2$.
The space of infinite binary sequences with the metric $d(x,y)=2^{-n}$, where $n$ is the first index at which $x$ and $y$ differ.
The [p-adic integers](c:p-adic-integer) $\mathbb Z_p$ are homeomorphic to Cantor space.
Non-example: The interval $[0,1]$ is compact and metrizable but connected, and Baire space $\mathbb N^{\mathbb N}$ is totally disconnected but not compact, so neither is Cantor space.

steps: Give $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ the metric $d(x,y)=2^{-n}$, where $n$ is the first index with $x_n\ne y_n$.
This metric induces the product topology, and it is complete, because every Cauchy sequence fixes each coordinate after some point.
The sequences that are eventually $0$ form a countable dense subset.
So Cantor space is separable and completely metrizable, which means it is a [Polish space](c:polish-space).
links.why: Results for Polish spaces, such as those of descriptive set theory, apply to Cantor space, which is the compact case.

reminder: Cardinal arithmetic defines the sum, product and power of cardinals through disjoint unions, products and function sets.
definition: For sets $A$ and $B$ with cardinalities $\kappa=|A|$ and $\lambda=|B|$, cardinal arithmetic defines $\kappa+\lambda=|A\sqcup B|$ through the [disjoint union](c:disjoint-union), $\kappa\cdot\lambda=|A\times B|$ through the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product), and $\kappa^\lambda=|A^B|$ through the [function set](c:function-set) of all functions $B\to A$. For finite [cardinal numbers](c:cardinal-number), these operations agree with the usual arithmetic of natural numbers.
examples: $\aleph_0+\aleph_0=\aleph_0\cdot\aleph_0=\aleph_0$, because $\mathbb N\sqcup\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$ are countable.
$2^{\aleph_0}=|\mathcal P(\mathbb N)|=|\mathbb R|$.
With the axiom of choice, $\kappa+\lambda=\kappa\cdot\lambda=\max(\kappa,\lambda)$ when $\kappa$ and $\lambda$ are nonzero and one of them is infinite.
Non-example: Ordinal addition is not cardinal addition, because $1+\omega=\omega\ne\omega+1$ for ordinals, but $1+\aleph_0=\aleph_0+1=\aleph_0$ for cardinals.

reminder: A Cartan decomposition splits a real semisimple Lie algebra into the $+1$ and $-1$ eigenspaces of a Cartan involution.
definition: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a real [semisimple Lie algebra](c:is-semisimple) and let $\theta$ be a Cartan involution of $\mathfrak g$, an involutive automorphism for which $-B(X,\theta Y)$ is positive definite, where $B$ is the Killing form. The Cartan decomposition is $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak k\oplus\mathfrak p$, where $\mathfrak k$ and $\mathfrak p$ are the $+1$ and $-1$ eigenspaces of $\theta$. For a connected semisimple [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ with finite center and this Lie algebra, every element is $k\exp X$ with $k$ in the maximal compact subgroup $K$ with Lie algebra $\mathfrak k$ and $X\in\mathfrak p$.
examples: For $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb R)$ with $\theta(X)=-X^T$, the space $\mathfrak k=\mathfrak{so}(n)$ holds the skew-symmetric matrices and $\mathfrak p$ holds the symmetric matrices with trace $0$.
On the group $SL_n(\mathbb R)$, this is the polar decomposition $g=k\,e^X$ with $k\in SO(n)$ and $X$ symmetric.
For $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb R)$, the space $\mathfrak k$ is spanned by $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathfrak p$ has dimension $2$.

Non-example: The Iwasawa decomposition $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak k\oplus\mathfrak a\oplus\mathfrak n$ has three summands, and $\mathfrak a\oplus\mathfrak n$ is a subalgebra that is not the $-1$ eigenspace of $\theta$, so it is not a Cartan decomposition.

reminder: A category of fibrant objects is a category with weak equivalences and fibrations in which every object is fibrant.
definition: A category of fibrant objects is a [category with weak equivalences](c:category-with-weak-equivalences) that also has a class of fibrations, which contains the isomorphisms and is closed under composition, and a [terminal object](c:terminal-object) $*$. Every map $X\to *$ is a fibration, [pullbacks](c:pullback) of fibrations exist and are fibrations, and pullbacks of fibrations that are weak equivalences are weak equivalences. Every object $X$ has a path object, a factorization of the diagonal $X\to X\times X$ into a weak equivalence followed by a fibration.
examples: The fibrant objects of a model category, with the fibrations and weak equivalences of the model structure, form a category of fibrant objects; the Kan complexes are the fibrant objects of simplicial sets.
Topological spaces with Serre fibrations and weak homotopy equivalences form a category of fibrant objects, where the path object of $X$ is $X^{[0,1]}$.
Non-example: Simplicial sets with Kan fibrations and weak equivalences do not form one, because $\Delta^1\to*$ is not a Kan fibration; only the Kan complexes do.

steps: Take a category of fibrant objects $C$.
Forget the fibrations, the terminal object and the path objects.
What remains is a [category with weak equivalences](c:category-with-weak-equivalences).
The fibrant case adds fibrations, pullbacks of fibrations and path objects, which give control of homotopy limits.
links.why: Results about categories with weak equivalences, such as the homotopy category, apply to a category of fibrant objects, which also has the tools of fibrations.

reminder: The Cauchy-Riemann equations say $u_x=v_y$ and $u_y=-v_x$ for the real and imaginary parts of $f=u+iv$.
definition: Let $f=u+iv$ be a function of $z=x+iy$ on an open subset of $\mathbb C$, where $u$ and $v$ are the [real part](c:real-part) and the imaginary part of $f$. The Cauchy-Riemann equations are the two equations $u_x=v_y$ and $u_y=-v_x$ for the [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative) of $u$ and $v$, and they are equivalent to $\partial f/\partial\bar z=0$. If $u$ and $v$ have continuous partial derivatives, then $f$ is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) exactly when it satisfies them.
examples: For $f(z)=z^2=(x^2-y^2)+i\,2xy$, we get $u_x=2x=v_y$ and $u_y=-2y=-v_x$.
The function $e^z=e^x\cos y+ie^x\sin y$ satisfies both equations.
Non-example: The function $f(z)=\bar z=x-iy$ has $u_x=1$ but $v_y=-1$, so the first equation fails.

reminder: The Čech nerve of a morphism $U\to X$ is the simplicial object of iterated fiber products of $U$ over $X$.
definition: Let $C$ be a [category](c:category) with [pullbacks](c:pullback) and let $p:U\to X$ be a morphism of $C$. The Čech nerve of $p$ is the [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) $\check C(U)$ whose object in degree $k$ is the $(k+1)$-fold fiber product $U\times_X\cdots\times_XU$. Its face maps omit one factor, and its degeneracy maps repeat one factor.
examples: For an open cover $\{U_i\}$ of a space $X$ and $U=\bigsqcup_iU_i$, the object in degree $k$ is $\bigsqcup U_{i_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{i_k}$.
For a surjection of sets $p:U\to X$, degree $1$ gives the equivalence relation $U\times_XU$ of pairs with the same image, and the nerve is the nerve of the matching groupoid.
For $X=*$, the Čech nerve of $U\to*$ has the object $U^{k+1}$ in degree $k$.
Non-example: The simplicial object with the ordinary products $U^{k+1}$ in degree $k$ is the Čech nerve of $U\to*$, but not of $p:U\to X$ when $X$ is not terminal.

steps: Take a morphism $p:U\to X$ and put $\check C_k=U\times_X\cdots\times_XU$ with $k+1$ factors.
For each monotone map $\theta:[m]\to[k]$, define $\check C_k\to\check C_m$ by the projections onto the factors $\theta(0),\dots,\theta(m)$.
These maps respect composition and identities of monotone maps.
So $\check C$ is a functor $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to C$, that is a [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) of $C$.
links.why: Every construction for simplicial objects, such as geometric realization, applies to the Čech nerve.

reminder: A cellular map between CW complexes sends the $n$-skeleton of its source into the $n$-skeleton of its target for every $n$.
definition: Let $X$ and $Y$ be [CW complexes](c:cw-complex) with $n$-skeletons $X^{(n)}$ and $Y^{(n)}$. A cellular map is a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $f:X\to Y$ with $f(X^{(n)})\subseteq Y^{(n)}$ for every $n\ge0$.
examples: The inclusion of a subcomplex $A\subseteq X$ is a cellular map.
The map $S^1\to S^1$, $z\mapsto z^2$, is cellular for the cell structure with one $0$-cell at $1$ and one $1$-cell, because it fixes the point $1$.
By the cellular approximation theorem, every continuous map between CW complexes is homotopic to a cellular map.
Non-example: Give $S^2$ one $0$-cell and one $2$-cell. An embedding $S^1\to S^2$ sends the $1$-skeleton of $S^1$ onto a circle, but the $1$-skeleton of $S^2$ is a point, so the map is not cellular.

steps: Take a cellular map $f:X\to Y$ between CW complexes.
By definition, $f$ is continuous as a map of the underlying topological spaces.
So $f$ is a [continuous function](c:continuous-function).
The cellular case adds the condition that $f$ maps each skeleton into the skeleton of the same dimension.
links.why: Facts about continuous functions, such as composition and homotopy, apply to cellular maps.

reminder: The centroid of a region is the average position of its points, which is its center of mass for uniform density.
definition: The centroid of a bounded region $R\subset\mathbb R^n$ with positive finite volume is the point $c=\frac1{|R|}\int_Rx\,dx$, the [integral](c:integral) average of its points. For finitely many points $p_1,\dots,p_k$, the centroid is their average $\frac1k\sum_ip_i$.
examples: The centroid of a [triangle](c:triangle) with vertices $A,B,C$ is $(A+B+C)/3$, the point where the three medians meet.
The centroid of a solid tetrahedron is the average of its four vertices, and it divides the segment from a vertex to the centroid of the opposite face in the ratio $3:1$.
The centroid of a half-disc of radius $r$ lies on its axis of symmetry at distance $4r/(3\pi)$ from the diameter.
Non-example: The circumcenter of a right triangle is the midpoint of its hypotenuse, which is not its centroid, because the centroid lies two thirds of the way along each median from its vertex.

reminder: A cevian is a line segment that joins a vertex of a triangle to a point on the line of the opposite side.
definition: Let $ABC$ be a [triangle](c:triangle). A cevian from the vertex $A$ is a line segment $AD$ where $D$ is a point on the line $BC$ that contains the opposite side. The point $D$ is the foot of the cevian.
examples: The median from $A$ is the cevian whose foot is the midpoint of $BC$.
The altitude from $A$ is the cevian whose foot is the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to the line $BC$.
The [angle bisector](c:angle-bisector) from $A$ is the cevian whose foot divides $BC$ in the ratio $AB:AC$.
Non-example: A midsegment joins the midpoints of two sides and does not start at a vertex, so it is not a cevian.

steps: Take a triangle $ABC$ and the [angle bisector](c:angle-bisector) from the vertex $A$.
The bisector meets the line $BC$ at a point $D$.
So $AD$ joins the vertex $A$ to a point on the line of the opposite side, and it is a cevian.
The angle bisector adds the condition that $\angle BAD=\angle DAC$.
links.why: Results about cevians, such as Ceva's theorem, apply to angle bisectors.

reminder: A chain condition says that chains in a partially ordered set cannot grow forever in one direction.
definition: Let $P$ be a set with a [partial order](c:partial-order), for example the set of submodules of a [module](c:module) ordered by inclusion. The ascending chain condition says that every chain $x_1\le x_2\le\cdots$ in $P$ is eventually constant, and the descending chain condition says the same for every chain $x_1\ge x_2\ge\cdots$.
examples: The ideals of $\mathbb Z$ satisfy the ascending chain condition but not the descending one, because $\mathbb Z\supsetneq2\mathbb Z\supsetneq4\mathbb Z\supsetneq\cdots$.
The subspaces of a finite-dimensional vector space satisfy both conditions, because the dimension changes along every strict chain.
The submodules of the Prüfer group $\mathbb Z[1/p]/\mathbb Z$ satisfy the descending chain condition but not the ascending one.

Non-example: The subspaces of an infinite-dimensional vector space satisfy neither condition; for an independent sequence $e_1,e_2,\dots$, the spans of $e_1,\dots,e_n$ grow strictly and the spans of $e_n,e_{n+1},\dots$ shrink strictly.

steps: Take a partially ordered set $P$ that satisfies the [ascending chain condition](c:ascending-chain-condition).
Every ascending chain in $P$ is then eventually constant.
So chains in $P$ cannot grow forever upward, which is a chain condition in the sense above.
A chain condition also covers the downward direction, which this case does not.
links.why: Results stated for chain conditions cover Noetherian modules, whose submodules satisfy the ascending chain condition.

steps: Take a partially ordered set $P$ that satisfies the [descending chain condition](c:descending-chain-condition).
Every descending chain in $P$ is then eventually constant.
So chains in $P$ cannot shrink forever downward, which is a chain condition in the sense above.
A chain condition also covers the upward direction, which this case does not.
links.why: Results stated for chain conditions cover Artinian modules, whose submodules satisfy the descending chain condition.

reminder: A change of measure replaces a probability measure $P$ by a measure $Q$ with $dQ=Z\,dP$ for a density $Z$.
definition: Let $P$ be a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) and let $Z\ge0$ be a random variable with $E_P[Z]=1$. The measure $Q(A)=E_P[Z\mathbf 1_A]$, written $dQ=Z\,dP$, is a change of measure of $P$. It is [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-measure) with respect to $P$, its [Radon-Nikodym derivative](c:radon-nikodym-derivative) is $Z=dQ/dP$, and expectations transform by $E_Q[X]=E_P[ZX]$.
examples: For $P=N(0,1)$ and $Z=e^{\theta x-\theta^2/2}$, the new measure is $Q=N(\theta,1)$, which shifts the mean by $\theta$.
By Girsanov's theorem, for a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $W$ under $P$ and $Z_T=\exp(\theta W_T-\theta^2T/2)$, the process $W_t-\theta t$ is a Brownian motion under $Q$.
Importance sampling estimates $E_P[X]$ by sampling from $Q$ and averaging $X\,dP/dQ$.
Non-example: The Dirac measure $\delta_0$ is not a change of measure of $N(0,1)$, because $\delta_0$ is not absolutely continuous with respect to $N(0,1)$, so it has no density.

reminder: The characteristic of a ring is the least positive $n$ with $n\cdot1=0$, or $0$ if there is no such $n$.
definition: The characteristic of a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is the nonnegative generator of the kernel of the unique ring homomorphism $\mathbb Z\to R$. Equivalently, it is the least $n\ge1$ with $1+\cdots+1=0$ ($n$ terms), or $0$ if $n\cdot1\ne0$ for all $n\ge1$. The characteristic of a [field](c:field) is $0$ or a [prime number](c:prime-number).
examples: The fields $\mathbb Q$, $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$ have characteristic $0$.
The finite field $\mathbb F_p=\mathbb Z/p$ and the field of rational functions $\mathbb F_p(t)$ have characteristic $p$.
The ring $\mathbb Z/n$ has characteristic $n$, and the [trivial ring](c:trivial-ring) has characteristic $1$.
Non-example: The number $6$ is not the characteristic of any field, because $(2\cdot1)(3\cdot1)=0$ would give zero divisors; it is the characteristic of the ring $\mathbb Z/6$.

steps: Take a [ring](c:ring) $R$ of [characteristic zero](c:char-zero), so that $n\cdot1\ne0$ for every $n\ge1$.
Then the kernel of the homomorphism $\mathbb Z\to R$ contains no positive integer, so it is $\{0\}$.
The nonnegative generator of $\{0\}$ is $0$, so the characteristic of $R$ is $0$.
So characteristic zero is the case where the characteristic has the value $0$.
links.why: A statement about rings of characteristic zero is the case $0$ of a statement about the characteristic.

reminder: The charge of a conserved current is its integral over a Cauchy surface, and it does not depend on the surface.
definition: Let $X$ be a [spacetime](c:spacetime) of dimension $n$ and let $J$ be a [conserved current](c:conserved-current) of a field theory, an $(n-1)$-form built from the fields and their derivatives with $dJ=0$ on solutions of the equations of motion. The charge of $J$ on a Cauchy surface $\Sigma$ is the [integral](c:integral) $Q_\Sigma(\phi)=\int_\Sigma J[\phi]$, evaluated on a solution $\phi$. When the fields decay fast enough at infinity, Stokes' theorem shows that $Q_\Sigma$ does not depend on the choice of $\Sigma$.
examples: For a free massless scalar field on Minkowski space, the energy current gives the charge $E=\int(\tfrac12\dot\phi^2+\tfrac12|\nabla\phi|^2)\,d^3x$.
For a complex scalar field with a $U(1)$ symmetry, the Noether current gives a charge proportional to $\int i(\bar\phi\dot\phi-\phi\dot{\bar\phi})\,d^3x$.
Non-example: A current $J$ with $dJ\ne0$ on solutions has an integral $\int_\Sigma J$ that depends on $\Sigma$, so it is not the charge of a conserved current.

reminder: A charted space is a topological space covered by open sets that are homeomorphic to open subsets of a model space.
definition: Let $H$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space), called the model space. A charted space modeled on $H$ is a topological space $M$ with an atlas, that is a set of charts $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$, each a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) from an [open set](c:open-set) $U\subseteq M$ onto an open subset of $H$, such that the sets $U$ cover $M$. The atlas needs no condition on the transition maps.
examples: Every open subset $U$ of $H$ is a charted space with the single chart $\mathrm{id}_U$.
The circle $S^1$ is a charted space over $\mathbb R$, with two angle charts that cover it.
Every [manifold](c:manifold) is a charted space modeled on $\mathbb R^n$, and a smooth manifold is a charted space whose transition maps are smooth.
Non-example: The figure eight is not charted over $\mathbb R$, because no neighborhood of the crossing point is homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb R$.

steps: Take a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ of dimension $n$ and a point $m\in M$.
Some open neighborhood of $m$ is homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$; take that homeomorphism as a chart.
These charts cover $M$, so $M$ is a charted space modeled on $\mathbb R^n$.
The manifold case adds that $M$ is Hausdorff and second countable, which a charted space does not require.
links.why: Definitions made for charted spaces, such as smooth structures, apply to every manifold.

reminder: The first Chebyshev function $\vartheta(x)$ is the sum of $\ln p$ over all primes $p\le x$.
definition: The first Chebyshev function is $\vartheta(x)=\sum_{p\le x}\ln p$, where the sum runs over the [prime numbers](c:prime-number) $p\le x$. The second Chebyshev function is $\psi(x)=\sum_{p^k\le x}\ln p$, which also counts the prime powers $p^k$ with $k\ge1$.
examples: $\vartheta(10)=\ln2+\ln3+\ln5+\ln7=\ln210$.
$\psi(10)=\ln(2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot7)=\ln2520$, which equals $\ln\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,10)$.
Non-example: The prime counting function $\pi(10)=4$ counts primes without the weights $\ln p$, so it is not a Chebyshev function; here $\vartheta(10)\approx5.35$.

reminder: Chern classes assign to each complex vector bundle $E$ classes $c_k(E)$ in $H^{2k}$ that are natural and multiplicative under direct sum.
definition: For a [complex vector bundle](c:complex-vector-bundle) $E\to X$, the Chern classes are the classes $c_k(E)$ in the [integral cohomology](c:integral-cohomology) group $H^{2k}(X;\mathbb Z)$, with total class $c(E)=1+c_1(E)+c_2(E)+\cdots$. They are natural, $c(f^*E)=f^*c(E)$, they satisfy the Whitney formula $c(E\oplus F)=c(E)c(F)$, and $c_k(E)=0$ for $k>\operatorname{rank}E$. They are normalized so that $c_1$ of the [tautological line bundle](c:tautological-line-bundle) on $\mathbb{CP}^\infty$ generates $H^2(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)$.
examples: For the tangent bundle of $\mathbb{CP}^n$, $c(T\mathbb{CP}^n)=(1+x)^{n+1}$, where $x$ generates $H^2$.
For a line bundle $L$, the class $c_1(L)\in H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$ classifies $L$ up to isomorphism.
Non-example: The Stiefel-Whitney class $w_1$ of a real bundle lies in $H^1(X;\mathbb Z/2)$, so it is not a Chern class, which has even degree and integer coefficients.

steps: A [characteristic class](c:characteristic-class) assigns to each bundle $E\to X$ of a given type a class in the cohomology of $X$, natural under pullback.
Assign to every complex vector bundle $E\to X$ the class $c_k(E)\in H^{2k}(X;\mathbb Z)$.
Naturality $c_k(f^*E)=f^*c_k(E)$ is one of the defining properties of Chern classes.
So $c_k$ is a characteristic class of complex vector bundles that also satisfies the Whitney sum formula.
links.why: Facts about characteristic classes, such as their definition by classifying maps, apply to Chern classes.

reminder: The circumcenter of a triangle is the point at equal distance from its three vertices.
definition: The circumcenter of a [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$ is the point $O$ with $OA=OB=OC$. It is the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the three sides, and it is the center of the [circumcircle](c:circumcircle) through $A$, $B$ and $C$.
examples: In a right triangle, the circumcenter is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.
In an equilateral triangle, the circumcenter and the [centroid](c:centroid) are the same point.
In an obtuse triangle, the circumcenter lies outside the triangle.
Non-example: The incenter has equal distance from the three sides, not from the three vertices, so it is not the circumcenter unless the triangle is equilateral.

reminder: Clebsch-Gordan coefficients express the irreducible summands of a tensor product of representations in the product basis.
definition: Let $\rho_{j_1}$ and $\rho_{j_2}$ be [irreducible representations](c:irreducible-representation) of a group such as $SU(2)$, with bases $\{e_m\}$ and $\{f_{m'}\}$. The [tensor product of representations](c:tensor-product-of-representations) $\rho_{j_1}\otimes\rho_{j_2}$ is [isomorphic](c:isomorphism) to a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) $\bigoplus_J\rho_J$ of irreducible representations, and the Clebsch-Gordan coefficients are the entries of this isomorphism in the product [basis](c:basis) $\{e_m\otimes f_{m'}\}$. For $SU(2)$, they are the numbers $\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|JM\rangle$ in $|J,M\rangle=\sum_{m_1+m_2=M}\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|JM\rangle\,|j_1,m_1\rangle|j_2,m_2\rangle$.
examples: In $\tfrac12\otimes\tfrac12=1\oplus0$, the singlet is $|0,0\rangle=(|{\uparrow\downarrow}\rangle-|{\downarrow\uparrow}\rangle)/\sqrt2$, so its Clebsch-Gordan coefficients are $\pm1/\sqrt2$.
The coefficient $\langle j_1j_1j_2j_2|j_1{+}j_2,j_1{+}j_2\rangle$ for the top state equals $1$.
The coefficient $\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|JM\rangle$ vanishes unless $M=m_1+m_2$ and $|j_1-j_2|\le J\le j_1+j_2$.

Non-example: The matrix entries of one irreducible representation $\rho_j$ in a basis, the Wigner $D$-functions, are not Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, because they do not relate a tensor product to its summands.

reminder: A subset of a topological space is closed when its complement is open.
definition: A [subset](c:subset) $C$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is closed when its complement $X\setminus C$ is an [open set](c:open-set). Equivalently, $C$ contains all of its limit points.
examples: In $\mathbb R$, the interval $[0,1]$, every single point and the set $\mathbb Z$ are closed.
The empty set and the whole space $X$ are closed in every topological space.
The zero set $f^{-1}(0)$ of a continuous function $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is closed.
Non-example: The interval $(0,1)$ is not closed in $\mathbb R$, because its complement $(-\infty,0]\cup[1,\infty)$ is not open.

reminder: A closed symmetric monoidal category is a symmetric monoidal category in which every functor $-\otimes Y$ has a right adjoint.
definition: A closed symmetric monoidal category is a [symmetric monoidal category](c:symmetric-monoidal-category) $(C,\otimes,I)$ in which, for every object $Y$, the [functor](c:functor) $-\otimes Y$ has a right [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) $[Y,-]$. That is, there are natural bijections $C(X\otimes Y,Z)\cong C(X,[Y,Z])$, and $[Y,Z]$ is the internal hom.
examples: The category of sets with the Cartesian product is closed, and $[Y,Z]=Z^Y$ is the set of functions from $Y$ to $Z$.
The category of vector spaces over a field $k$ with $\otimes_k$ is closed, and $[Y,Z]=\mathrm{Hom}_k(Y,Z)$.

Non-example: The category of topological spaces with the product is symmetric monoidal but not closed, because $-\times Y$ does not preserve quotient maps for some spaces $Y$, so it has no right adjoint.

steps: Take a closed symmetric monoidal category $(C,\otimes,I)$.
By definition, $(C,\otimes,I)$ with its symmetry is a [symmetric monoidal category](c:symmetric-monoidal-category).
So forgetting the internal hom leaves a symmetric monoidal category.
The closed case adds a right adjoint $[Y,-]$ for every functor $-\otimes Y$.
links.why: Everything about symmetric monoidal categories holds here, and the internal hom adds a way to turn morphisms into objects.

steps: Take a [cartesian closed category](c:cartesian-closed-category) $C$ with finite products, where each functor $-\times Y$ has a right adjoint $[Y,-]$.
Use the product as $\otimes$ and the terminal object as the unit $I$.
The swap of factors is a symmetry, so $C$ is a symmetric monoidal category.
Each functor $-\otimes Y$ has the right adjoint $[Y,-]$, so $C$ is closed symmetric monoidal.
links.why: A theorem about closed symmetric monoidal categories applies to sets, spaces of functions and other cartesian closed categories.

reminder: A coadjoint orbit is an orbit of the coadjoint action of a Lie group on the dual of its Lie algebra.
definition: Let $G$ be a [Lie group](c:lie-group) with [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g$. The group acts on the [dual space](c:dual-space) $\mathfrak g^*$ by the [coadjoint action](c:coadjoint-action) $(g\cdot\xi)(X)=\xi(\mathrm{Ad}_{g^{-1}}X)$. A coadjoint orbit is an [orbit](c:orbit) $G\cdot\xi$ of this action.
examples: For $G=SO(3)$, we have $\mathfrak g^*\cong\mathbb R^3$, and the coadjoint orbits are the origin and the spheres centered at the origin.
For an abelian Lie group, the coadjoint action is trivial, so every coadjoint orbit is a single point.

For $G=U(n)$, identify $\mathfrak g^*$ with the Hermitian matrices; the orbit of $\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ is the set of Hermitian matrices with these eigenvalues, a flag manifold when the $\lambda_i$ differ.

Non-example: An orbit of the adjoint action on $\mathfrak g$ is not a coadjoint orbit, because it lies in $\mathfrak g$ and not in $\mathfrak g^*$; the two agree only when an invariant inner product identifies $\mathfrak g$ with $\mathfrak g^*$.

steps: Take a Lie group $G$ and its coadjoint action on $\mathfrak g^*$, which is an action of $G$ on a set.
For $\xi\in\mathfrak g^*$, the set $G\cdot\xi=\{g\cdot\xi:g\in G\}$ is an [orbit](c:orbit) of this action.
So every coadjoint orbit is an orbit of a group action.
The coadjoint case fixes the action to be the coadjoint action on $\mathfrak g^*$.
links.why: Facts about orbits, such as the bijection $G/G_\xi\to G\cdot\xi$ with the stabilizer, apply to coadjoint orbits.

reminder: A cochain complex is a sequence of objects with differentials $d:V^n\to V^{n+1}$ such that $d\circ d=0$.
definition: A cochain complex $V^\bullet$ of [modules](c:module) over a ring is a sequence of modules $V^n$ with maps $d^n:V^n\to V^{n+1}$, called [differentials](c:differential), such that $d^{n+1}\circ d^n=0$ for every $n\in\mathbb Z$. It is a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) with the degrees reversed, so that the differential raises the degree.
examples: The [de Rham complex](c:de-rham-complex) $\Omega^0(M)\to\Omega^1(M)\to\Omega^2(M)\to\cdots$ of a smooth manifold, with the exterior derivative as differential.
The singular cochains $C^n(X;A)=\mathrm{Hom}(C_n(X),A)$ of a space $X$, with the coboundary map.
Non-example: The sequence $\cdots\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{1}\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{1}\mathbb Z\to\cdots$ has $d\circ d=1\ne0$, so it is not a cochain complex.

steps: Take a cochain complex $(V^n,d^n)$ with $d^{n+1}d^n=0$.
Put $V_n=V^{-n}$ and $d_n=d^{-n}:V_n\to V_{n-1}$.
Then $d_{n-1}\circ d_n=0$, so $(V_n,d_n)$ is a [chain complex](c:chain-complex).
The cochain convention keeps the original indexing, in which the differential raises the degree.
links.why: Everything known for chain complexes, such as homology, applies after this reindexing, and cohomology is the homology of the reindexed complex.

reminder: A category is cocomplete when every diagram indexed by a small category has a colimit.
definition: A [category](c:category) $C$ is cocomplete if every diagram $F:D\to C$ indexed by a [small category](c:small-category) $D$ has a [colimit](c:colimit) in $C$. Equivalently, $C$ has all small coproducts and all coequalizers.
examples: The categories of sets, groups, abelian groups, topological spaces and small categories are cocomplete.
Every presheaf category $\mathrm{Set}^{\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}}$ on a small category $\mathcal C$ is cocomplete.
Non-example: The category of finite sets has all finite colimits but not all small ones; the coproduct of countably many one-point sets is infinite, so it does not exist there.

steps: Take a [bicomplete category](c:bicomplete-category) $C$, which has all small limits and all small colimits.
In particular, every small diagram in $C$ has a colimit.
So $C$ is cocomplete.
Cocompleteness drops the requirement on limits.
links.why: A result about cocomplete categories applies to every bicomplete category, such as the category of sets.

steps: Take a cocomplete category $C$.
Every finite category is small, so every finite diagram in $C$ has a colimit.
So $C$ has all finite colimits, and it is [finitely cocomplete](c:finitely-cocomplete-category).
Cocompleteness adds the colimits of infinite small diagrams.
links.why: Every fact about finite colimits applies to a cocomplete category.

reminder: A bilinear form $a$ is coercive when $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$ for some constant $\alpha>0$ and all $v$.
definition: Let $V$ be a real [normed space](c:normed-space), usually a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space), and let $a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form). The form $a$ is coercive when there is a constant $\alpha>0$ with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$ for every $v\in V$. For a complex space with a sesquilinear form, the condition is $\operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$.
examples: The inner product of a Hilbert space is coercive with $\alpha=1$.
The Dirichlet form $a(u,v)=\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\,dx$ is coercive on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ for a bounded domain $\Omega$, by the Poincaré inequality.
The form $a(u,v)=\int_\Omega(\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+uv)\,dx$ is coercive on $H^1(\Omega)$ with $\alpha=1$.
Non-example: The Dirichlet form is not coercive on $H^1(\Omega)$, because $a(1,1)=0$ for the constant function $1$.

steps: Take a coercive bilinear form $a$ with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$.
Then the functional $v\mapsto a(v,v)$ is at least $\alpha\|v\|^2$.
This tends to infinity as $\|v\|\to\infty$, so the functional is coercive in the sense of [coercivity](c:coercivity).
The bilinear case gives the explicit quadratic bound $\alpha\|v\|^2$.
links.why: General facts about coercivity apply to the form, and the bilinear case adds an explicit constant $\alpha$.

steps: Take a coercive bounded bilinear form $a$ with constant $\alpha$ on a Hilbert space $V$.
Define $A:V\to V^*$ by $\langle Au,v\rangle=a(u,v)$.
Then $\langle Au,u\rangle/\|u\|=a(u,u)/\|u\|\ge\alpha\|u\|$, which tends to infinity as $\|u\|\to\infty$.
So $A$ is a [coercive operator](c:coercive-operator).
links.why: Results for coercive operators, such as the Browder-Minty theorem, apply to the operator of a coercive form.

reminder: An operator $A:X\to X^*$ is coercive when $\langle Ax,x\rangle/\|x\|$ tends to infinity as $\|x\|$ tends to infinity.
definition: Let $X$ be a real [Banach space](c:banach-space) with [dual space](c:dual-space) $X^*$ and [norm](c:norm) $\|\cdot\|$, and let $A:X\to X^*$ be an operator. The operator $A$ is coercive when $\langle Ax,x\rangle/\|x\|\to\infty$ as $\|x\|\to\infty$, where $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the duality pairing.
examples: The identity map of a Hilbert space, seen as a map to its dual, is coercive, because $\langle x,x\rangle/\|x\|=\|x\|$.

The $p$-Laplacian $u\mapsto-\operatorname{div}(|
abla u|^{p-2}
abla u)$ on $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ with $p>1$ is coercive, because $\langle Au,uangle=\|
abla u\|_p^p$.
Non-example: The zero operator is not coercive, because $\langle0,x\rangle/\|x\|=0$ for every $x$.

steps: Take a [coercive bilinear form](c:coercive-bilinear-form) $a$ on a Hilbert space $V$ with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$.
Define the operator $A:V\to V^*$ by $\langle Au,v\rangle=a(u,v)$.
Then $\langle Au,u\rangle/\|u\|\ge\alpha\|u\|$, which tends to infinity as $\|u\|\to\infty$.
So $A$ is coercive, and the operator case allows nonlinear operators and weaker growth.
links.why: The Browder-Minty theorem for coercive operators covers the linear problems of coercive bilinear forms.

steps: Take a coercive operator $A:X\to X^*$.
For large $\|x\|$, the ratio $\langle Ax,x\rangle/\|x\|$ exceeds $1$, so $\langle Ax,x\rangle\ge\|x\|$.
So $\langle Ax,x\rangle\to\infty$ as $\|x\|\to\infty$, and the functional $x\mapsto\langle Ax,x\rangle$ has the property of [coercivity](c:coercivity).
The operator case measures this growth against the norm $\|x\|$.
links.why: General facts about coercivity apply to the operator, which has the stronger growth against the norm.

reminder: Coercivity says that a form, operator or functional grows without bound as the norm of its argument grows.
definition: Let $V$ be a [normed space](c:normed-space). A [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $a$ on $V$ is coercive when $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$ for some $\alpha>0$, an operator $A:V\to V^*$ into the [dual space](c:dual-space) is coercive when $\langle Av,v\rangle/\|v\|\to\infty$ as $\|v\|\to\infty$, and a functional $J:V\to\mathbb R$ is coercive when $J(v)\to\infty$ as $\|v\|\to\infty$. Each version says that the quantity controls the norm of $v$.
examples: The Dirichlet form $\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx$ is coercive on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ for a bounded domain $\Omega$.
On a Hilbert space, the functional $J(v)=\|v\|^2-\ell(v)$ with $\ell$ bounded and linear is coercive, because $J(v)\ge\|v\|^2-\|\ell\|\,\|v\|$.
Non-example: The function $J(x)=\sin x$ on $\mathbb R$ is bounded, so $J(x)$ does not tend to infinity as $|x|\to\infty$ and $J$ is not coercive.

steps: Take a [coercive bilinear form](c:coercive-bilinear-form) $a$ with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$.
Then the functional $v\mapsto a(v,v)$ is at least $\alpha\|v\|^2$.
This tends to infinity as $\|v\|\to\infty$, so the functional is coercive.
The bilinear case adds the explicit quadratic lower bound $\alpha\|v\|^2$.
links.why: A result stated for coercivity covers coercive bilinear forms, such as the Dirichlet form.

steps: Take a [coercive operator](c:coercive-operator) $A:V\to V^*$, so $\langle Av,v\rangle/\|v\|\to\infty$ as $\|v\|\to\infty$.
For large $\|v\|$, this ratio exceeds $1$, so $\langle Av,v\rangle\ge\|v\|$.
So $\langle Av,v\rangle\to\infty$, and the functional $v\mapsto\langle Av,v\rangle$ is coercive.
The operator case says how fast the functional grows compared with the norm.
links.why: A result stated for coercivity covers coercive operators, such as the $p$-Laplacian.

reminder: An object of a model category is cofibrant when the map from the initial object to it is a cofibration.
definition: Let $M$ be a [model category](c:model-category) with [initial object](c:initial-object) $\emptyset$. An [object](c:object) $X$ of $M$ is cofibrant when the unique map $\emptyset\to X$ is a [cofibration](c:cofibration).
examples: In simplicial sets with the Kan-Quillen model structure, every object is cofibrant, because $\emptyset\to X$ is a monomorphism.
In topological spaces with the Quillen model structure, every CW complex is cofibrant, for example the sphere $S^n$.
In chain complexes of modules with the projective model structure, every bounded-below complex of projective modules is cofibrant.
Non-example: In chain complexes of abelian groups with the projective model structure, the group $\mathbb Z/2$ in degree $0$ is not cofibrant, because $\mathbb Z/2$ is not projective.

steps: Take a [bifibrant object](c:bifibrant-object) $X$, which is both cofibrant and fibrant.
In particular, the map $\emptyset\to X$ is a cofibration.
So $X$ is cofibrant.
Bifibrant adds the condition that $X\to*$ is a fibration.
links.why: A result about cofibrant objects applies to every bifibrant object, which is the object type used in many homotopy computations.

reminder: A coherent topos is a category of sheaves on a small coherent site with the coherent coverage.
definition: A coherent topos is a [Grothendieck topos](c:grothendieck-topos) that is equivalent to the category of sheaves on a small [coherent category](c:coherent-category) with its [coherent coverage](c:coherent-coverage), in which the covering families are the finite jointly epimorphic families. In particular, the terminal object of a coherent topos is compact: every covering of it has a finite subcovering.
examples: The topos of sets is coherent.
For a profinite group $G$, the topos of sets with a continuous action of $G$ is coherent.
For a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme $S$, the étale topos of $S$ is coherent.
Non-example: The topos of sheaves on $\mathbb R$ is not coherent, because its terminal object is not compact; the cover of $\mathbb R$ by the intervals $(-n,n)$ has no finite subcover.

steps: Take a coherent topos $\mathcal E$.
By definition, $\mathcal E$ is equivalent to the sheaves on a small coherent site.
A small site gives a [Grothendieck topos](c:grothendieck-topos), so $\mathcal E$ is one.
The coherent case adds that the site is coherent, with finite covering families.
links.why: Every fact about Grothendieck toposes holds for a coherent topos, which adds finiteness and compactness.

reminder: A commutative C*-algebra is a C*-algebra in which $ab=ba$ for all elements $a$ and $b$.
definition: A commutative C*-algebra is a [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) $A$ with $ab=ba$ for all $a,b\in A$. By Gelfand duality, every such algebra is isometrically $*$-isomorphic to $C_0(X)$ for a locally compact Hausdorff space $X$, the [Gelfand spectrum](c:gelfand-spectrum) of $A$.
examples: The algebra $C_0(X)$ of continuous complex functions on a locally compact Hausdorff space $X$ that vanish at infinity, with the supremum norm and complex conjugation.
The algebra $\mathbb C^n$ with componentwise operations and the maximum norm.
The algebra $L^\infty(\mu)$ for a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$.
Non-example: The matrix algebra $M_2(\mathbb C)$ is a C*-algebra but not commutative, because $E_{12}E_{21}\ne E_{21}E_{12}$.

steps: Take a commutative C*-algebra $A$.
By definition, $A$ is a [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra).
So every theorem about C*-algebras applies to $A$.
The commutative case adds the condition $ab=ba$ for all $a,b\in A$.
links.why: General C*-algebra results apply, and commutativity adds the identification with continuous functions.
